clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in NR3C1 encoding the glucocorticoid receptor, reducing tissue sensitivity to cortisol
There is high circulating cortisol and ACTH but, crucially, no Cushingoid phenotype because the tissues cannot respond to the excess
The compensatory ACTH drive stimulates adrenal overproduction of mineralocorticoids and androgens, producing the clinical features
Mineralocorticoid excess causes hypertension and hypokalaemic alkalosis, while androgen excess causes hirsutism, acne, menstrual disturbance, and precocious puberty or virilisation
The diagnosis rests on hypercortisolaemia with preserved (though upwardly reset) diurnal rhythm and resistance to dexamethasone suppression, in the absence of Cushingoid features
Management uses high-dose synthetic glucocorticoid with predominant glucocorticoid activity to suppress ACTH and thereby reduce the mineralocorticoid and androgen excess
Suspect the syndrome when biochemical hypercortisolism coexists with hypertension and androgen excess but no clinical Cushing syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: The glucocorticoid receptor mediates the cellular actions of cortisol, including negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Loss-of-function variants in NR3C1 reduce receptor number or function, so tissues are relatively resistant to cortisol. Impaired feedback allows ACTH to rise, which in turn drives the adrenal cortex to secrete more cortisol; because peripheral tissues remain unresponsive, the raised cortisol does not produce Cushingoid changes. The heightened ACTH stimulation also increases production of adrenal steroids with mineralocorticoid activity (such as deoxycorticosterone) and adrenal androgens, and the excess cortisol can spill over onto the mineralocorticoid receptor. This explains the combination of hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis and features of androgen excess despite normal or elevated cortisol.
additionalDifferentials: Polycystic ovary syndrome (for the androgen features)
Primary hyperaldosteronism (for the hypertension and hypokalaemia)
Familial or acquired abnormalities of cortisol-binding globulin
additionalInvestigations: Serum cortisol and ACTH showing elevated levels without Cushingoid features
Midnight cortisol and diurnal profiling demonstrating an upwardly reset but preserved rhythm
Dexamethasone suppression testing showing relative resistance to suppression
Serum potassium, renin, and adrenal androgen and mineralocorticoid precursor measurement
24-hour urinary free cortisol interpreted against the absence of clinical Cushing syndrome
redFlags: Severe or resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia
Marked virilisation or precocious puberty in children
Adrenal hyperplasia or incidental adrenal enlargement from chronic ACTH drive
Fatigue and features suggesting relative tissue cortisol deficiency during stress
reference.prognosis: With appropriate synthetic glucocorticoid therapy to suppress ACTH, blood pressure, electrolytes, and androgen-related features usually improve and the outlook is good; untreated disease carries the cardiovascular risks of chronic hypertension and the consequences of androgen excess.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the biochemical hypercortisolism as Cushing syndrome despite the absent phenotype
Overlooking mineralocorticoid excess as the cause of hypertension and hypokalaemia
Attributing the androgen features to polycystic ovary syndrome alone
Failing to appreciate that affected tissues may be relatively cortisol-deficient under stress
